entries.title: Price tag for US war in Iran barrels past $48 billion
entries.summary: A Pentagon budget officer has said the price of the Iran war surpassed $48.3 billion last week. That does not include costs sustained in Iranian attacks on US bases — lawmakers want details the Pentagon is loath to give.
entries.content:
United States of America

Price tag for US war in Iran barrels past $48 billion

November 20, 2026

A Pentagon budget officer has said the price of the Iran war surpassed $48.3 billion last week. That does not include costs sustained in Iranian attacks on US bases — lawmakers want details the Pentagon is loath to give.

The cost of the US war in Iran, which Donald Trump launched without Congressional approval on February 28, blew past $48.3 billion (€44 billion) on November 13, according to Pentagon budgetary official Arthur Miller.

Miller laid out the figures during Thursday testimony before the US Senate Armed Services Committee as his nomination to become Navy comptroller is considered.

Miller said the costs cover US military operations, equipment and munitions but not damage sustained at US military installations across the Middle East.

How much damage has Iran inflicted on US military installations in the Middle East?

According to news agency AP, damage to hundreds of aircraft hangars, barracks, radar systems, warehouses and other US military infrastructure has run up into the billions of dollars, however, Miller failed to provide an estimate of the total cost when pressed during the hearing.

Committee Chairman Roger Wicker, a Republican from Mississippi, called on Miller to provide the figures as soon as possible.

In October, the Wall Street Journal cited Pentagon sources who said damage to US facilities in the region could range from $5 billion to as much as $15 billion.

The Washington-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies put the cost for repairing buildings alone — excluding equipment and systems inside — at more than $4 billion.

A war by any name, is still a very expensive undertaking

The Trump administration has variously argued that the war is not a war, that it has been won, and that it will be over soon. There is currently no end in sight and on top of the US military's costs, the global economy is getting pummeled every day as a result of the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz — which is the direct result of US attacks on the Islamic Republic.

The Trump administration is calling on Congress to pass the Pentagon's $1.5 trillion 2027 defense budget — a 40% increase over 2026 — in order to fund America's military. Unlikely prior to the November 3 midterm elections, the prospects of that figure being approved now that Democrats have taken control of both houses of Congress from Republicans would seem nigh impossible.

entries.title: New Ukraine talks including Europe to be held 'soon' — Merz
entries.summary: Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz says European leaders could take part in fresh Ukraine talks on "neutral ground." The UK and EU countries have urged a seat at the table in meetings between the US, Russia and Ukraine.
entries.content:
Ukraine

New Ukraine talks including Europe to be held 'soon' — Merz

November 20, 2026

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz says European leaders could take part in fresh Ukraine talks on "neutral ground." The UK and EU countries have urged a seat at the table in meetings between the US, Russia and Ukraine.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Friday he believes new talks regarding Russia's invasion of Ukraine with European leaders taking part will occur "soon."

What did Merz say about the next Ukraine talks?

"Of course we are prepared to hold talks with Russia, we have always said this. These talks are now set to take place soon," Merz said after a meeting of Ukraine's allies in Berlin. He did not give a concrete date for the next talks, but said Europe's interests would be represented by Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was present at the Coalition of the Willing summit in the German capital, along with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.   

Merz said the talks including Europe would take place on "neutral ground," such as the United Arab Emirates.

Merz along with other European leaders have been critical of meetings between US, Ukrainian and Russian representatives regarding the conflict, arguing that Europe needs a direct seat at the negotiating table.

Putin, in talks with Trump, says European leaders invited to Moscow

Russia's invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, with the Trump administration prioritizing an end to the war.

Trump took part in a bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Friday, with Trump saying the two leaders would discuss the war in closed-door talks. Putin acknowledged that Europeans want a seat at the table, and said Russia invited European leaders to Moscow.

"We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without Europeans," Putin said, while rejecting any military cooperation between Europe and Ukraine. 

Merz: 'Yalta format cannot bring peace' to Ukraine

Trump also took part in a historic trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. 

The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting raised fears that the US, Russia and China are looking to carve up the world into spheres of influence. It drew comparisons with the February 1945 Yalta Conference, where US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Union leader Joseph Stalin discussed Europe's future as Nazi Germany's defeat was imminent in World War II.   

Following the Trump-Xi-Putin summit, Merz said a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine. He downplayed the Shenzhen summit between the three leaders as a "photo opportunity."

Merz handed out pieces of the Berlin Wall to leaders at the Coalition of the Willing summit, saying the Yalta structure had brought "oppression, insecurity and a lack of peace."

"This is exactly what Yalta stood for," Merz said.

The Yalta format sought to divide post-war Germany into four zones: US, UK, France and the USSR. This later led to the construction of the Berlin Wall dividing the city into West and East Berlin, with city residents attempting to cross the barrier shot dead by border guards.

entries.title: 'Humanitarian mission' for Kostiantynivka: Is it a trap?
entries.summary: Russian President Putin has proposed an evacuation of the Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka, like the recent operation in Oleshky. Experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?
entries.content:
Ukraine

'Humanitarian mission' for Kostiantynivka: Is it a trap?

November 19, 2026

Russian President Putin has proposed an evacuation of the Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka, like the recent operation in Oleshky. Experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

What is the situation for civilians?

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Humanitarian proposals as leverage

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.

Ceasefire as military tactic

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

How should Kyiv respond to Moscow's proposal?

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

entries.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
entries.summary: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.
entries.content:
November 19, 2026

Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production. 

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

Ramping up electricity production

As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar. 

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."

Drilling for oil

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls. 

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities. 

Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue. 

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition. 

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."

This interview also appeared as a video.

entries.title: Germany news: Pistorius visits Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
entries.summary: Germany's defense minister's first stop in Poland was the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Pistorius visits Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip

Published November 19, 2026last updated November 20, 2026

Germany's defense minister's first stop in Poland was the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Defense Minister Boris Pistorius talks security in Poland
  • Germany warns of cybersecurity risks in gadgets
  • UniCredit and Germany reach Commerzbank takeover agreement
  • Berlin brings together leaders of European countries and US envoys for talks on Ukraine

We've closed the blog. Below is a roundup of the biggest headlines from Germany on Thursday, November 19.

Skip next section Thank you for reading

Thank you for reading

We're closing the blog today after a busy day in Berlin. We'll be back tomorrow with the latest headlines. Tschüss!

Skip next section European allies back Ukraine's borders at 'Coalition of the Willing' summit in Berlin

European allies back Ukraine's borders at 'Coalition of the Willing' summit in Berlin

European powers rallied behind Ukraine at a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin earlier today.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz emphasized that he wanted European powers to play a role in bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.

"We know that this war will only end if there is a diplomatic solution," Merz said after the meeting in the German capital on Thursday.

"But this war must end with a Ukraine that preserves its territorial integrity, has strong security guarantees on its side and is above all embedded in European security," he added.

Skip next section IG Metall blasts VW 'catalog of horrors' ahead of collective bargaining talks

IG Metall blasts VW 'catalog of horrors' ahead of collective bargaining talks

IG Metall, Germany's largest union, railed against automaker Volkswagen's latest demands on its workforce days before both sides are set to begin collective bargaining talks next Tuesday.



The union described VW's vision for the future of work at the Wolfsburg-based giant as a "catalog of horrors."

VW, the world's second-largest car company by both sales and production, has seen profits nosedive — it announced quarterly losses of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) in October — for a number of reasons, ranging from increased competition to tariffs and soft sales. Now the company plans to slash 120,000 jobs at 10 brands by 2030.

Arguing that its financial outlook has "deteriorated," VW management says it has no choice but to make deeper cuts faster than expected.

VW wants to scrap the current contract's 35-hour week and is demanding employees work overtime without pay if needed and went so far as to announce that pay would be "adjusted" if workers were forced to work fewer than 35 hours. Moreover, it is calling for a pay freeze for 2027-2028, as well as cuts to benefits for long-term employees.

IG Metall says workers haven't seen a raise since May 2024 and is calling for a 5% hike now, citing ever-rising living costs.

Regional IG representative Thorsten Gröger said, "VW management is stabbing its employees the back." He added that negotiations will be "tenacious, bitter and exhausting" and that they "will leave deep scars at the company."

Workers are primed for walkouts, with the union warning that the battle may be far larger than anything VW has ever seen. 

VW works council chairwoman Daniela Cavallo, who represents employees within the company, said, "Management's promises are obviously worthless." Cavallo said workers felt "betrayed" after they agreed to major job cuts for the health of the company two years ago.

The current contract applies to some 130,000 employees at German production sites in Braunschweig, Chemnitz, Dresden, Emden, Hanover, Kassel, Salzgitter, Wolfsburg and Zwickau.

Skip next section German defense minister call Auschwitz a 'warning' to all of us

German defense minister call Auschwitz a 'warning' to all of us

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Thursday called on Europeans to be vigilant against far-right extremism and warned of divisions and labels in society.

Speaking during a visit to Auschwitz-Birkenau, a former concentration camp, Pistorius said the site bore witness to the worst of Nazi Germany's crimes, calling it an absolute low point.  

"It all started with defining what made a life unworthy; by dividing according to race, origin, faith, sexual orientation," Pistorius warned, saying that such marginalization was experiencing a "renaissance" and "gaining ground with far-right extremist parties across Europe."

The defense minister said Auschwitz provides all people, but particularly Germans, with a "symbol warning that we all bear responsibility for what happens and what must not be allowed to happen."

During his tour of the camp, Pistorius laid a wreath at its death wall, where Nazi soldiers shot roughly 5,000 prisoners dead, and lit a candle at the victims' memorial.

Before he departed the site, Pistorius expressed his wish that more German students and travel groups would visit the camp "than appears to be the case at present."

Skip next section AfD politician accuses Le Pen of abandoning party 'core'

AfD politician accuses Le Pen of abandoning party 'core'

The deputy chairman of Germany's right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) has accused French presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen of deserting her core values in her bid to achieve wider popularity and improve her chance of victory in French presidential elections. 

For years, Le Pen claimed to be embarking on a policy of what's often called "de-demonization," trying to shed the extreme-right image of her father and predecessor, Jean-Marie Le Pen, and soften the stance of the party now called the National Rally or RN.

"Mrs. Le Pen, whom we all once admired greatly, now seems to have one fundamental principle: I say whatever the polls demand of me," Sven Tristschler told the right-leaning website The Pioneer.

France is headed into the last months of a presidential election campaign, with incumbent Emmanuel Macron's second and final term coming to an end and no clear candidate emerging as a main challenger to Le Pen as yet.

"At the end of the day, her victory would likely be even more catastrophic for the right than her defeat," Tritscher asserted. "The citizens would think they were voting to the right, only to get another Macron in the end."

He said that in hindsight, he was glad the AfD and RN parties had fallen out in European politics in recent years, and said AfD supporters should not anticipate a similar move toward moderation.

"A hollowing-out will not take place with us," he said, using the German scientific term for enucleation, the removal of the internal nucleus or core of a cell.

The AfD has made similar complaints about Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, accusing her party of a process of "Melonization" involving a softening of its core policy stances in a bid to retain power.

A similar power struggle is thought to be brewing within the AfD itself as it remains far adrift of majority support despite regularly polling as the largest single party in Germany at present.

Skip next section Bundesbank expects inflation to rise in 2027

Bundesbank expects inflation to rise in 2027

Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, said in its monthly report that inflation in Germany will rise "sharply" at the beginning of 2027. 

Inflation could remain stable through the end of the year, given that a fuel tax cut is still keeping a lid on prices.

Inflation had fallen to 2.9% from 3.3% in September after the German government introduced the fuel discount.

But the central bank said the expiration of that fuel tax cut, along with other government measures, would drive inflation higher.

The report also highlighted that natural gas prices are expected to rise.

"On top of this, higher energy and input costs are expected to gradually feed through into the prices of other goods and certain services," the Bundesbank said.

Skip next section Deutche Telekom to invest in French AI company

Deutche Telekom to invest in French AI company

German telecommunications firm, Deutsche Telekom, announced that it will invest €100 million ($109.75 million) in French start-up Mistral AI, Europe's largest artificial intelligence company.

The investment will pour into Mistral from Telekom's subsidiary T.Capital Tech Fund.

Telekom said the move is a first step toward a strategic partnership, where the two firms plan to jointly support companies and the public sector in Germany in introducing tailored AI.

"Europe’s competitiveness depends on our ability to develop and use powerful AI," Telekom board member Ferri Abolhassan said in a statement announcing the deal. "Businesses must be able to trust this technology while retaining control over their data."

The move is the latest investment by Telekom in the AI space. In February, Telekom built an AI factory in Munich, which has since been expanded due to high demand.

Skip next section Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin

Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Berlin for a summit of the "Coalition of the Willing." The group, which represents Kyiv's allies, is expected to push for a deeper European role in any efforts to end the war.

The process has so far been dominated by the US, Russia and Ukraine.

Zelenskyy wrote on X that "we are doing everything we can to ensure that Europe's presence in the negotiation process is fully represented."

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff flew to Germany to attend the summit at the Chancellery.

Skip next section German teen suspected of planning mosque attack with 3D printer weapons

German teen suspected of planning mosque attack with 3D printer weapons

An 18-year-old in western Germany has been held in pre-trial detention in Germany since August over the alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack on a mosque, prosecutors have said.

The teen, who is from the town of Eslohe in North Rhine-Westphalia, allegedly held far-right extremist views and was planning the attack for late 2026 or early 2027, senior public prosecutor Alexandra Wiese said.

"He also directed his racist ideology against people of the Muslim faith," Wiese told public broadcaster WDR.

A search of the suspect's home led investigators to find numerous weapons, weapon parts and ammunition, including items manufactured using a 3D printer.

Wiese did not provide details of potential targets in order to protect possible victims.

No charges have yet been filed against the teen and Wiese stressed that the presumption of innocence applies as the investigation continues.

Skip next section UniCredit and Germany reach agreement on Commerzbank takeover

UniCredit and Germany reach agreement on Commerzbank takeover

Italian commercial bank UniCredit and the German government reached agreement on the big sticking points of its takeover of Commerzbank.

The EU greenlit UniCredit's takeover of Germany's Commerzbank earlier this week.

The merging of ​UniCredit and Commerzbank would create a bank with more than €1.3 trillion ($1.4 trillion) in assets

across two of the eurozone's largest economies.

It would be one of the most significant cross-border ​European banking deals in years.

In a statement to Reuters news agency, Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said Germany "supports a swift process and an orderly transition of control."

"We have reached common ground and UniCredit has ‌made clear commitments to Germany as a business location, to the rights of

Commerzbank employees and to a continued constructive dialogue with ‌the works ​council," Klingbeil said, referring to a body of elected employee representatives.

Among the concessions, Germany is said to have given up its insistence on naming two supervisory board members to Commerzbank.

Meanwhile, UniCredit agreed to the key German demand to keep UniCredit's enlarged German business headquartered and listed in Frankfurt.

UniCredit also reportedly pledged to put German nationals on UniCredit's board of directors.

Skip next section Defense Minister Boris Pistorius heads to Poland

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius heads to Poland

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will travel to Poland for a two-day visit.

Pistorius is scheduled to meet his Polish counterpart, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, in the capital, Warsaw, for talks on defense policy.

Poland is a member of both the EU and NATO and is one of the most important political and military allies of Ukraine.

The trip to Germany's neighbor to the east will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.

Auschwitz-Birkenau is one of the biggest symbols of the Holocaust and Germany's Nazi regime, with some 1.1 million people having died in the camp between 1940 and 1945, most of them Jews.

The camp's victims were shot, murdered in gas chambers or died of starvation and disease.

Correction: An earlier version of this update misidentified the German defense minister. We apologize for the error.

Skip next section Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets

Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets

The German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) said in a report that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals.

According to the report, the number of hacked systems has nearly doubled within a year, with BSI reporting some 75,400 infected systems in Germany to internet providers every day, an 89% increase. Some of the gadgets were found to be already infected at the factory, the report says.

The vast majority of cases involved Android devices, particularly consumer electronics connected to the so-called "Internet of Things."

BSI said criminals rent the hijacked devices as proxy botnets on the dark web to hide their own attacks, which would allow for consumers themselves to unknowingly come under investigators' scrutiny.

BSI President Claudia Plattner has also warned of AI-driven attacks.

"The disruption coming in particular from high-performance, agentic AI has set new benchmarks," she said.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will head to Poland today to talk security with one the most important political and military allies of Ukraine.

His trip will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.

Meanwhile, Germany's Federal Office for Information Security has warned that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals

Follow this blog for more on that and other stories from Germany!

entries.title: Iraq's risky standoff: The state vs. Iran-allied militias
entries.summary: This week, Iraqi security forces surrounded an area run by the Kataib Hezbollah militia. Onlookers describe it as the most dangerous confrontation between the Iraqi state and Iran-allied militias in decades.
entries.content:
Iraq

Iraq's risky standoff: Government vs. Iran-allied militias

November 19, 2026

This week, Iraqi security forces surrounded an area run by the Kataib Hezbollah militia. Onlookers describe it as the most dangerous confrontation between the Iraqi state and Iran-allied militias in decades.

For years, there have all kinds of rumors about Jurf al-Sakhar, an area around 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the Iraqi capital Baghdad. It is controlled by an Iraqi militia called Kataib Hezbollah, that's closely allied with Iran, and no Iraqi government troops or news media outlets have been allowed inside for around 12 years.

Rumors about what's happening in the area include allegations about secret prisons, mass graves, drone and weapons manufacturing and storage, as well as criminal activity such as oil smuggling. Jurf al-Sakhar is also allegedly a base for foreign, Hezbollah-supporting nationals from Iran, Yemen, Bahrain and Lebanon.

Recently two people —  an Israeli researcherand a US journalist — who were kidnapped by an Iraqi militia are thought to have been held captive in this area.

Jurf al-Sakhar previously had an estimated 89,000 residents but after the extremist group known as the "Islamic State," or IS, rose to power in Iraq in 2014, much of the population was displaced in fighting. The area was eventually taken over by Kataib Hezbollah, a militia that had fought IS alongside other armed groups.

As a collective, the armed groups are referred to as the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF. Not all of them have pledged allegiance to Iran but Kataib Hezbollah, a Shiite Muslim majority group, has.

In the past 12 years, tens of thousands of the displaced people from here, mostly Sunni Muslims, have not been allowed to return and the area has been described as militarized.

Its name was even changed by Kataib Hezbollah fighters, from Jurf al-Sakhar ("rocky bank") to Jurf al-Nasr ("bank of victory").

'Not even over our dead bodies'

But recent events may shake Kataib Hezbollah's hold on this area.

An early November report for the Iraqi government says that since 2021, the group has smuggled hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, siphoned from pipelines around Jurf al-Sakhar.

Kataib Hezbollah denies this.

Iraq's new government, headed by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, made several arrests based on the report and demanded that Kataib Hezbollah leave Jurf al-Sakhar by Friday, Nov. 20.

Kataib Hezbollah rejected al-Zaidi's ultimatum, with a spokesperson saying the group would not withdraw "not even over our dead bodies."

Al-Zaidi then ordered state security forces to surround the area, while Hezbollah reportedly brought in reinforcements.

Observers have described the standoff as one of the most consequential and riskiest confrontations between an Iraqi government and Iranian-backed militiasin Iraq in more than two decades.

"It is a political signal that things will change, that he [al-Zaidi] wants to disarm militias, integrate them into state and claim back the state's authority," Ulf Laessing, head of the Syria and Iraq project for Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, or KAS, told DW. "But it's a minefield and he needs to navigate carefully."

The standoff is also the result of long-running political tensions in Iraq, where the state is torn between its US allies on the one hand and Iranian allies on the other. Both hold sway in Iraq and are considered important relationships.

During Donald Trump's presidency of the US, and thanks to the US and Israel's war with Iran, there's been more pressure on Iraq to disarm Iran's allies inside the country. Al-Zaidi has set a deadline of next June to bring all weapons under the state's control.

Tensions, fears grow

The situation in Jurf al-Sakhar became even more tense this week. Al-Zaidi announced a new security plan for the area that involves other members of the PMF, state security forces and the police. Kataib Hezbollah rejected the plan.

"Al-Zaidi appears serious about ending Kataib Hezbollah's autonomous control of Jurf al-Sakhar," Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW. "Deploying federal forces and now establishing a new security command there shows this has moved beyond rhetoric."

But how dangerous is Kataib Hezbollah really? After all, al-Zaidi was actually nominated for the prime minister's job by a political bloc known as the Coalition Framework, or CF — these are the politicians who represent the PMF in parliament. Kataib Hezbollah's political party, Harakat Huqooq, is part of the CF.

And other researchers have been critical on social media, noting that the PMF troops that will be given partial control over Jurf al-Sakhar (should Kataib Hezbollah withdraw) are associated with that group anyway.

But Iraqi news media have also reported that there are divisions inside the CF, and apparently even within Kataib Hezbollah, about how to deal with the current standoff. Reportedly, some senior officials think that parts of Jurf al-Sakhar could be handed to federal forces in a gradual withdrawal, the London-based outlet Amwaj Media reported earlier this week, while some senior members of Kataib Hezbollah would seemingly prefer to hand the territory over to certain PMF brigades rather than to state security forces.

What will happen next?

Late Thursday afternoon, the news agency Reuters reported that, according to three anonymous officials, all parties had come to an agreement that would allow government forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.

A compromise is good because it avoids violence, KAS' Laessing said. "It might not be what al-Zaidi initially hoped for but it's still a political signal."

If it did come to actual fighting, the Iraqi military has more resources than Kataib Hezbollah, al-Shakeri explained. "[It] could probably take Jurf al-Sakhar if the political leadership and security institutions remained united," he said. "But there would be no easy victory. Kataib Hezbollah does not need to defeat the Iraqi army conventionally. It can impose costs through asymmetric attacks, political pressure and its networks inside the state."

How the reported compromise plays out in the coming days, will also impact other Iraqi militias and they will be watching closely. Because "the core issue is whether a faction can continue controlling territory and economic activity beyond effective government oversight," al-Shakeri explained.

"The most likely compromise may be to remove Kataib Hezbollah's monopoly rather than remove the PMF from Jurf al-Sakhar altogether," he continued. "That would still matter if it opened the area to regular state forces, if it protects the oil infrastructure and places security under a clearer government command structure."

It could also lead to displaced residents being allowed back to their homes.

"But if one PMF faction simply replaces another while retaining its own networks and autonomy, then Zaidi has redistributed armed influence rather than fundamentally resolved the problem," al-Shakeri concluded.

entries.title: European leaders present united front in push for peace in Ukraine
entries.summary: Talks in Berlin end with reaffirmed support for Kyiv and a concerted push for European representation at future peace talks to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
entries.content:
Ukraine

European leaders present united front in push for peace in Ukraine

Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026

Talks in Berlin end with reaffirmed support for Kyiv and a concerted push for European representation at future peace talks to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

These updates have been closed.

Below, you can review the top news from the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin on Thursday, 19th November, below:

  • Ukraine's main European allies met in Berlin for 'Coalition of the Willing' talks
  • Leaders of Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy gathered following talks involving President Donald Trump, Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in China
  • US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were also at the meeting to brief allies about discussions in China
  • Ukraine's European allies are pushing to be included in US-backed negotiations with Russia

Skip next section Leaders of Germany, France, UK, Ukraine issue joint statement

Leaders of Germany, France, UK, Ukraine issue joint statement

Ukraine and three of its key European allies have reiterated their commitment "towards a comprehensive, just and lasting peace for Ukraine," which they described as being "vital for the security of Europe."

In a joint statement issued after Coalition of the Willing talks in Berlin, the leaders of Germany, France, the UK and Ukraine condemned  Russia's "systematic escalation of its deliberate and indiscriminate missile and drone attacks against Ukraine's civilians and civilian infrastructure."

Ukraine's right to defend itself was highlighted, as were Russia's battlefield losses.

The four leaders condemned "Russian hybrid attacks across Europe" and said they "would increase their resolve to strengthen the defence of Ukraine, Europe and NATO."

Leaders pledged "long-term and comprehensive support" for Kyiv and said that Ukraineäs air defense capability was a priority.

Russia's funding of its war effort would be targeted through sanctions and "pressure on Russian oil and gas revenues," while efforts to impede Russia's shadow fleet would continue.

On Ukraine's security, the leaders said the country needed "robust and legally binding security guarantees in place, once a ceasefire enters into force."

The statement mentioned "a European-led Multinational Force Ukraine composed of contributions from willing nations and supported by the US," something that has proven to be a sticking point for Russia.

The leaders said they supported "direct dialogue" between Kyiv and Moscow with US and European participation.

Ukraine's right to choose its own security arrangements needed to be "fully respected," the joint statement said.

"As a first step towards a cessation of hostilities, the leaders called on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire for the duration of the winter," the statement read.

Skip next section Message of European unity 'relayed to President Trump' — Jared Kushner

Message of European unity 'relayed to President Trump' — Jared Kushner

US special envoy Jared Kushner said unity in Europe was clear in the talks and that support for Ukraine remained strong.

"What we came away from today with is really seeing that Europe is very united and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine," Kushner said. "We relayed this to President Trump."

Kushner said this would also be relayed to the Russian delegation and that there was "a real desire for peace."

Kushner said that Trump had joined the Berlin meeting by phone and provided an update on the talks in Shenzhen with President Putin and President Xi.

"He sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage with both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said.

Kushner told reporters the talks with European leaders ⁠and ​Ukrainian President ​Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "made a lot ​of progress ‌on what those security ​guarantees ⁠can look like," as well ⁠as ​a post-war prosperity plan.

He also said Russia was "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war.

Skip next section Macron says question of Ukraine's NATO accession should be reopened

Macron says question of Ukraine's NATO accession should be reopened

French President Emmanuel Macron said that amid Russia's continued attacks on infrastructure and "maximalist demands," the first priority was for Ukraine to be able to defend itself.

Macron said allies needed to ensure that Ukraine had everything it needed to resist and defend itself from Russian attacks.

"Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO," Macron said in Berlin.

"Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now," the French leader insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.

Macron said security guarantees were a "key element for our long-term negotiations" and the security plan it had already submitted should remain.

Skip next section Zelenskyy says next round of talks must include Europe

Zelenskyy says next round of talks must include Europe

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Europe should be part of talks going forward.

"America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation at the negotiations is necessary," Zelenskyy said.

Zelenskyy said his country needed international support ahead of another winter and added that more work was needed to "push Russia to be more constructive in any negotiations."

He also said much work was done to make the Berlin meeting "as concrete as possible."

Zelenskyy thanked all partners and expressed gratitude to Germany, France, the UK, the US along with those who had come out in support of Ukraine.

Zelenskyy highlighted the importance of air defense and said that Russia's aerial bombardments were steadily intensifying.

Zelenskyy said there was no sign this would change as "the Russians have rejected every single proposal for de-escalation."

Zelenskyy said that it was "crucial" that the US "exerts influence on Russia."

Skip next section Merz pushes for European representation in peace talks

Merz pushes for European representation in peace talks

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pushed for Europe to play a role in helping secure peace in the war in Ukraine.

"Today we prepared for ourselves for possible peace talks," Merz said.

"These talks should comprise Ukraine, Russia, the United States and Europe," Merz said, adding that this format offered the best chance of securing peace.

The German leader said Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy would speak on behalf of Europe.

He went on to call the trilateral talks between the president of the United States, Russia and China today at an APEC summit a "photo op" and said such a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine.

Merz pledged "powerful support" for Ukraine in 2027 and mentioned the €45 billion earmarked for next year by the European Commission.

Merz said the level of support was being provided in order for Ukraine to be able to protect itself and that allies wanted the war to end.

Skip next section Outcome of Ukraine war will 'shape security in Europe' — Merz

Outcome of Ukraine war will 'shape security in Europe' — Merz

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the future of European security would be molded by what was happening in Ukraine.

"The outcome of this war will shape security in Europe for a long time to come," Merz said in a post on social media platform X.

"Together with our partners, we continue our support for peace in Ukraine. That's why we came together today for the Coalition of the Willing," Merz said.

He accompanied his comments with pictures from roundtable talks of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin.

Skip next section Zelenskyy says he discussed 'key issues' with German, French and British leaders

Zelenskyy says he discussed 'key issues' with German, French and British leaders

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he went over "key issues and needs" with German, French and British leaders.

Zelenskyy shared a video on X of his meeting with France's Emmanuel Macron, Britain's Andy Burnham and Germany's Friedrich Merz.

He said they discussed "countering Russian shahed drones and missiles, protecting the energy sector and infrastructure, as well as the diplomatic efforts."

"It is important that today's Coalition of the Willing meeting and bilateral meetings with leaders deliver results," he added.

Skip next section 'Coalition of the Willing' meeting in Berlin

'Coalition of the Willing' meeting in Berlin

Ukraine's European allies are gathering in Berlin in a show of support just hours after three-way talks took place involving the presidents of the US, Russia and China at the APEC summit.

European leaders are pushing to be included in US-backed talks to end the fighting in Ukraine with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and the US president's son-in-law Jared Kushner in Berlin for Thursday's meeting.

"Mr. Putin is not our friend and will never ​be," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a comment aimed at US President Donald Trump, who referred to Putin as "my friend" at a meeting on Wednesday.

"I find it very incomprehensible that a US president wants to sit down with President Putin," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told ​reporters.

"I think Putin will be even more emboldened after today's meeting. He looks happy," she added. "Unfortunately, that is not a good sign for world ​peace. That is not ‌a good sign for Ukraine ... And therefore I think that what will come out of this is that he will hit us Europeans even harder, unfortunately."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU was united in its support for Ukraine.

"Only through strength can we achieve a just and durable peace," she wrote on X. "We will maintain our support for Ukraine. And maintain full pressure on Russia. Europe stands strong and united."

Skip next section WATCH: Can Germany make Europe pay more for Ukraine?

WATCH: Can Germany make Europe pay more for Ukraine?

Germany's push for more European aid for Ukraine is triggering a backlash.

Michaela Küfner discusses charges of "blackmail" against Chancellor Merz together with DW colleagues Nina Haase, Max Hofmann and Teri Schultz.

Skip next section Putin not considering Black Sea truce after Kerch bridge strikes

Putin not considering Black Sea truce after Kerch bridge strikes

Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow would not hold off on strikes in the Black Sea region or on energy infrastructure following strikes by Ukraine on the Kerch bridge.

The crucial road and railway crossing linking the Crimean peninsula with mainland Russia was put out of action by a series of Ukrainian strikes.

"But after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, there will ⁠be no ​agreements. We will respond to these ​strikes. And I want everyone to know this: I believe ​our response will ‌be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge," he ​said.

Putin said ⁠the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to ⁠transport military ​equipment, as Kyiv has alleged.

"We will, of course, restore the bridge. The road section suffered serious damage," Putin said.

Skip next section Putin calls any European-Ukraine military ties 'a problem' for Russia

Putin calls any European-Ukraine military ties 'a problem' for Russia

Russian President Vladimir Putin said it would be unacceptable for there to be military cooperation between Ukraine and the EU, including any potential deployment of European troops to the country.

"Military cooperation in any form is, of course, a problem," Putin said at a press conference in China.

Putin also said European officials have been invited to Moscow to discuss the potential structure of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.

"The American side is urging us to agree to the involvement of the Europeans ... Through diplomatic channels, we suggested to the Europeans to come to Moscow. And after that we will decide in what format the talks can continue," Putin told reporters.

"We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans," Putin added.

For months, European politicians have emphasized that they should be present at any talks on the future of Ukraine.

Skip next section Leaders start to arrive

Leaders start to arrive

Leaders such as Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy, France's Emmanuel Macron, the UK's Andy Burnham, as well as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived Thursday at the chancellery in Berlin for the talks.

They were received by Chancellor Friedrich Merz ahead of discussions on providing support to Ukraine against Russia's war.

The “Coalition of the Willing” was established in early 2025 to back Ukraine. It has since grown to include nearly 40 countries, from Japan and Canada to Poland.

Skip next section Zelenskyy arrives in Berlin for summit

Zelenskyy arrives in Berlin for summit

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Berlin on Thursday for the so-called "Coalition of the Willing" meeting.

"Ukraine's priorities are strengthening our air defense, energy and financial support, the diplomatic track, and the next steps toward ending the war and guaranteeing security," he said in an online post.

He said different forms of meeting will take place, with a format involving the US side and European national security advisors.

The coalition is a grouping of countries that provide support to Ukraine against Russian aggression.

Leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy, as well as NATO head Mark Rutte and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will attend the meeting today.

Skip next section Ukraine claims responsibility for third attack on Kerch bridge

Ukraine claims responsibility for third attack on Kerch bridge

The Ukrainian military on Thursday claimed responsibility for a strike on the Kerch Bridge.

The bridge was attacked on Wednesday for a third time this week, halting rail traffic briefly and damaging some sections.

In an online post, the Ukrainian military said that the strike had been carried out by its forces using Neptune coastal missiles.

It stated that the strikes on Russian bridges hamper Moscow's ability to transport military supplies to the front line.

The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.

Skip next section Prince Harry says he would return to military service to fight Russia if needed

Prince Harry says he would return to military service to fight Russia if needed

The United Kingdom's Prince Harry said on Thursday he would rejoin the military to fight against Russia if needed.

"If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel," he said in an interview from Ukraine with The Telegraph.

"I think there's a lot that the whole world can learn from Ukraine," the prince said during an unannounced visit to the western city of Lviv over the weekend.

Prince Harry, a former British Army officer and the younger son of King Charles III, traveled to Ukraine for his fourth visit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, where he met with wounded veterans and medical staff.

"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, that doesn't mean that we're not at war," he told the UK newspaper.

He emphasized that "Ukraine are winning" and "there is no version where Russia is making any more advances"

entries.title: Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have held trilateral talks ― but what did they achieve?
entries.summary: The presidents of China, the US and Russia have held an unprecedented summit. While Trump said the three leaders were "making history," Xi described the talks as "fruitful" and Putin called them "open and candid."

entries.title: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
entries.summary: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.
entries.content:
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026

One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.

Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft. 

This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.

The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey. 

It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.

The draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, said negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.

Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.  

"This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he said in a statement.

'Worst fears' on climate financing

Another hotly contested issue at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.  

The second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion). It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035. 

The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world."

"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," said Raman.

The European Union has said it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.

What else is in the draft text?

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change. 

It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."

Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand."

The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.

The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."

Talks in crunch time

The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.

Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.

On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demand for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate the potent greenhouse gas methane.

The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

Australian Energy Minister Bowen said he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.

"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a plan we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming."

The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people. 

It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

The conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.

Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such asa Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.

"It's critically important for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," said David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

entries.title: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
entries.summary: Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.
entries.content:
November 19, 2026

Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.

Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange. 

Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.

The stock opened at $111.50 — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion.

The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months. 

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.

This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

First of the AI giants to go public

Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI,  has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027. 

Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.

Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.

That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.
